text:
“Madame, I have just come to Besançon for the first time in my life; I should very much like to have, and pay for, a piece of bread and a cup of coffee.”

The young lady smiled a little and then blushed; she feared, for this handsome young man, the ironic attention and jests of the billiard players. He would be frightened and would never return.

“Sit here beside me,” she said, showing him a marble table almost entirely hidden by the enormous mahogany counter that projected into the room.

The young lady leaned out from behind the counter, which gave her the opportunity to display a superb figure. Julien noticed it; all his thoughts changed. The beautiful young lady had just placed before him a cup, some sugar, and a small bread roll. She hesitated to call a waiter to bring coffee, fully understanding that when the waiter arrived, her tête-à-tête with Julien would end.

Lost in thought, Julien compared this cheerful blonde beauty with certain memories that often stirred him. The thought of the passion of which he had been the object took away almost all his timidity. The beautiful young lady had only a moment; she read it in Julien’s eyes.

“This pipe smoke is making you cough; come and have breakfast tomorrow before eight in the morning; then I am almost alone.”

“What is your name?” said Julien, with the caressing smile of happy timidity.

“Amanda Binet.”

“Will you allow me to send you, in an hour, a little parcel about this size?”

The beautiful Amanda reflected for a moment.

“I am watched: what you are asking of me may compromise me; nevertheless, I am going to write my address on a card, which you will put on your parcel. Send it to me without fear.”

“My name is Julien Sorel,” said the young man; “I have neither relatives nor acquaintances in Besançon.”

“Ah! I understand,” she said joyfully, “you have come for the law school?”

“Alas, no,” Julien replied; “I am being sent to the seminary.”

The most complete discouragement extinguished the animation in Amanda’s features; she called a waiter: she had courage now. The waiter poured coffee for Julien without looking at him.

Amanda was taking money at the counter; Julien was proud of having dared to speak: a quarrel broke out at one of the billiard tables. The shouts and denials of the players, resounding through that immense room, made a din that astonished Julien. Amanda was pensive and kept her eyes lowered.

“If you wish, Mademoiselle,” he suddenly said to her with assurance, “I shall say that I am your cousin.”

This little air of authority pleased Amanda. He is not an insignificant young man, she thought. She said to him very quickly, without looking at him, for her eye was occupied in seeing whether anyone was approaching the counter:

“I am from Genlis, near Dijon; say that you too are from Genlis, and that you are my mother’s cousin.”

“I shall not fail to do so.”

“Every Thursday at five o’clock in summer, the gentlemen from the seminary pass here in front of the café.”

“If you think of me when I pass, have a bouquet of violets in your hand.”

Amanda looked at him in astonishment; that look changed Julien’s courage into boldness; nevertheless, he blushed deeply as he said to her:

“I feel that I love you with the most violent love.”

“Do speak more softly,” she said to him with a frightened air. Julien was trying to recall the phrases from an odd volume of the New Heloise that he had found at Vergy. His memory served him well; for ten minutes he had been reciting the New Heloise to Mademoiselle Amanda, who was delighted; he was happy in his bravery, when suddenly the beautiful woman from Franche-Comté assumed an icy expression. One of her lovers had appeared at the door of the café.

He approached the counter, whistling and swaggering with his shoulders; he looked at Julien. At once, the latter’s imagination, always running to extremes, was filled with nothing but thoughts of a duel. He turned very pale, pushed his cup away, assumed a confident expression, and looked at his rival very attentively. As this rival lowered his head while familiarly pouring himself a glass of brandy at the counter, Amanda ordered Julien with a glance to lower his eyes. He obeyed and, for two minutes, remained motionless in his place, pale, resolute, and thinking only of what was about to happen; he was truly admirable at that moment. The rival had been astonished by Julien’s eyes; after swallowing his glass of brandy in one draught, he said a word to Amanda, put both hands into the side pockets of his heavy frock coat, and approached a billiard table, puffing and looking at Julien. The latter rose, carried away by anger; but he did not know how to go about being insolent. He put down his little parcel and, with the most swaggering air he could manage, walked toward the billiard table.

In vain prudence told him: But with a duel as soon as you arrive in Besançon, your ecclesiastical career is ruined.

What does it matter? It shall not be said that I let an insolent fellow escape me.

Amanda saw his courage; it made a charming contrast with the naïveté of his manners; in an instant, she preferred him to the tall young man in the frock coat. She rose and, while appearing to follow with her eyes someone passing in the street, quickly came and placed herself between him and the billiard table:

“Take care not to look askance at that gentleman; he is my brother-in-law.”

“What do I care? He looked at me.”

“Do you want to make me unhappy? No doubt he looked at you; perhaps he is even going to come and speak to you. I told him that you are a relative of my mother’s and that you have just arrived from Genlis. He is from Franche-Comté and has never gone beyond Dole on the road to Burgundy; so say whatever you like, and do not be afraid.”

Julien was still hesitating; she added very quickly, her counter-girl’s imagination supplying her with lies in abundance:

“No doubt he looked at you, but it was at the moment when he was asking me who you are; he is a man who is boorish with everyone; he did not mean to insult you.”

Julien’s eye followed the supposed brother-in-law; he saw him buy a number in the pool being played at the farther of the two billiard tables. Julien heard his loud voice shout in a threatening tone, “I’ll take the shot.” He passed swiftly behind Mademoiselle Amanda and took a step toward the billiard table. Amanda seized him by the arm:
